Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
Megan Calloway is a 30-year-old married woman who works as a bank teller at a mid-sized branch in suburban Ohio. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician, and she arrived at the intake appointment visibly tense, her gaze directed consistently toward the floor.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Megan was taken from her car in a parking garage late one evening by two men. Over the course of several hours in an unfamiliar location, she was subjected to sustained physical and psychological torture. Her captors moved around her slowly and deliberately, watching her reactions as they inflicted pain, sometimes going silent for long stretches before resuming. At various points they made threats of a sexual nature, and the assault included sexual violence. She was eventually left in a field and found by a passing driver. She had not spoken publicly about the full extent of what occurred until her disclosure to her physician several weeks ago.

In the months following the attack, Megan returned to work because she believed that stopping would mean something had permanently broken inside her. But the branch environment, which she had once found routine and manageable, became a source of sustained distress. Customers stand across the counter and look directly at her for the duration of each transaction. She had come to experience that sustained gaze — the ordinary, expectant eye contact of someone waiting to be helped — as something threatening and exposing, an echo of the way her captors had watched her with such deliberate attention. She began angling her face slightly downward while processing transactions, a habit her supervisor eventually noticed and commented on, leading to a formal conversation about professionalism that left Megan feeling humiliated and misunderstood. She has not told anyone at work what happened to her.

When a customer raises their voice — even in the mild, impatient tone common to busy afternoons at the counter — Megan's body responds before her mind catches up. Her chest tightens, her hands become unsteady on the keyboard. She is certain, in those moments, that something is about to escalate beyond her control. The same response arrives at home. Her husband, a generally even-tempered man, occasionally expresses frustration aloud — about traffic, about work — and Megan finds herself unable to remain in the room. She has not explained why she leaves. He has noticed, and the distance between them has grown in ways neither has fully named. Intimacy has become almost entirely absent from their marriage. Megan avoids sexual situations not because she has decided to but because her body will not allow her to stay present in them. She was certain, for a time, that this meant she was permanently changed in a way that could not be repaired.

Unusual silences unsettle her in a way that is difficult for her to articulate. At home, when the house goes quiet — no television, no ambient noise — she feels a specific, gathering dread, as though the silence is a precursor to something terrible arriving. She wakes most nights and moves through the house checking that the doors are locked, that nothing has changed. She returns to bed but rarely sleeps again before morning.

When the memory of the attack returns, it does not arrive as a recollection. It arrives as an event. The smell of cold concrete, the quality of the light, the particular texture of fear in her body — all of it reconstitutes without warning, triggered sometimes by nothing she can identify in advance. When this happens at work, she has had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she sits until she can breathe steadily again. She has also, over the past several months, begun spending impulsively — clothing, household items she doesn't need — in the hours after a particularly difficult day. She has come to understand this as a way of filling something, though she cannot say exactly what.

What finally brought Megan to seek help was her husband asking, quietly and without anger, whether she still wanted to be married to him. She did not know how to answer. What she hopes for, more than anything, is to be able to look someone in the eye again without flinching.
